title: How many statements a connection can hold
impact: Three read-path caches are keyed by SQL text and capped at 32 entries — the C per-connection prepared-statement cache, the per-worker Dart `schemaCache`, and the pool's row-size memory — and none of the three numbers had ever been measured, because every benchmark in the repo uses under ten distinct SQL strings. Exp 071 and exp 073 each rejected a cache change on exactly those grounds and each closed by asking for a `64 rotating query shapes, cache at capacity` workload before any cache-sizing experiment; neither built it, and exps 207 and 248 went after the lookup path instead, so the cache's scan has been attacked twice and its size never once. Exp 266 made the gap load-bearing two days before this run: under round-robin a sequential loop over D distinct statements was partitioned across four connections, each seeing ~D/4, and sticky dispatch sends the whole cycle to one. Because these caches evict at the front and promote on hit — approximately LRU, the worst policy for a cyclic scan — the cap is a cliff and not a slope: at D <= 32 every read hits, and at D = 33 the entry each read needs is the one the previous miss evicted. Raising all three caps to 128 is a reproduced -55.5% / -55.1% / -53.3% at 40, 64 and 128 rotating statements (14.0 us per read to 6.1 us), flat across that range exactly as a cliff predicts, with every lane inside the old cap neutral in two independent order-flipped collections and peak RSS up 0.8-1.2 MB against a ~30 MB floor. The load-bearing lane is the adversarial one: `churn-unique`, which never repeats a statement so no cache of any size can help, measured a reproduced +42.1% on the first candidate and would have rejected the raise on its own. The cause was `stmt_cache_insert` compacting the array on every eviction — `(STMT_CACHE_MAX - 1) x ~1.6 KB`, so 50 KB per prepare at 32 entries and 203 KB at 128 — identified by arithmetic (39 MB/sample of extra traffic against a measured 1.53 ms) before a second measurement was taken. Reclaiming the LRU slot in place instead, which gives up no ordering the promote-by-swap had not already given up, took the same lane to a reproduced -11.9%, because the baseline was paying ~640 us of its 3688 us sample to shift 12.8 MB. Five tests push 400 distinct statements through every cache and check each statement's identity from its result (its row, its projection, its parameter arity), since a cache returning the wrong entry is silent rather than fatal; four of the five were verified to fail against a deliberately mismatched entry. The cliff moves rather than disappears, and what bounds the next raise is the fixed-size `read_tables[64]` / `dep_columns[64]` arrays that make an entry 1.6 KB when a typical statement reads one table.
